title: Separate setup helpers from VCS shim
rationale: Dispatcher setup/install behavior is stack-specific setup logic rather than VCS branching logic, so it should live outside the git compatibility shim.

name: Tighten QA/finalize validation loops
description: Developer prompt now forbids unrelated test copying, QA reports must include npm test command/count evidence, and finalize distinguishes modified-file failures from pre-existing unrelated failures so branch-ready is blocked without wasting a developer retry.

name: Finalize phase outputs
description: Finalize now uses FINALIZE_VALIDATION.md as the workflow verdict artifact while still writing FINALIZE_REPORT.md for operational push/rebase details.

title: Refinery jj rebases must stay on the backend path
rationale: Refinery previously ran raw git rebase <target> <branch> from the repo root even in colocated jj repos, which broke the branch-ready invariant by validating one merge path in finalize and a different path in refinery. Rebased jj runs should go through VcsBackend.rebase() in the run workspace so finalize and refinery share backend semantics.

title: Finalize failure must not infer success from missing mail
rationale: agent-worker onPipelineComplete previously treated missing finalize phase-complete/agent-error mail as success, which allowed finalize FAIL verdicts to enqueue merge work and reach refinery. The worker must preserve the pipeline success=false result when finalize mail is absent.

name: Keep orchestrator tests aligned with runtime validation contracts
description: Pipeline epic tests need QA fixture reports with npm test command text and pass/fail counts so qaReportHasTestEvidence() treats PASS/FAIL verdicts as valid. Refinery migration tests should assert backend mergeWithoutCommit()/getConflictingFiles() behavior rather than raw git --squash shell calls.

title: Ignore detached HEAD branch labels for dispatch and merge targeting
rationale: Detached workspaces can surface HEAD as the current branch, but branch:HEAD is not a real merge target. Rejecting it at branch-label extraction/application prevents dispatcher from persisting stale branch:HEAD labels and makes refinery fall back to the real default or explicit target branch instead of failing the no-commits guard against HEAD.

title: Skip branch-ready when troubleshooter already landed the branch
rationale: A finalize failure can still be recoverable by the troubleshooter, but if that recovery directly lands the work on the target branch, enqueueing the run to merge queue and emitting branch-ready causes a false no-commits merge failure. After troubleshooter recovery, agent-worker should detect zero diff versus the target branch, close the task, and skip merge queue / branch-ready.

content: Troubleshooter prompts and tool-facing JSON should use task/taskId terminology. Keep legacy taskId only as a compatibility alias for internal runtime fields and older tool callers, not as the primary language shown to agents or operators.

description: In colocated jj repos, JujutsuBackend.detectDefaultBranch() and getCurrentBranch() cannot rely on main/master or raw working-copy change IDs. During a dirty working copy on dev, getCurrentBranch() returned the unbookmarked jj change ID (for example yozrpnkmlxpq), and run/auto-merge threaded that into merge targeting. Refinery then reported no-commits against the change ID instead of the real trunk.
resolution: Honor git-town.main-branch and origin/HEAD before bookmark-name fallbacks in detectDefaultBranch(), and in getCurrentBranch() fall back to the parent revision's bookmark before returning a jj change ID.

title: Finalize pre-existing test failures should reconcile to merged when already landed
rationale: A finalize verdict of tests_failed_pre_existing_issues does not necessarily mean the task failed to land. In jj/git workflows the branch may already match the target branch by the time finalize reports the deterministic failure. In that case agent-worker should mark the run merged and close the task instead of recording a failed run that contradicts repository state.

description: Finalize retry suppression depended on parseFinalizeFailureScope(), but the parser only recognized inline '## Failure Scope: ...' or plain '- UNRELATED_FILES' formatting. Real finalize artifacts used section formatting with bold bullets ('## Failure Scope' then '- **UNRELATED_FILES**'), so the parser returned unknown and pipeline-executor incorrectly sent Finalize Feedback - Retry N back to developer.
resolution: Accept bold bullet section formatting in parseFinalizeFailureScope() so UNRELATED_FILES is recognized from real finalize artifacts and finalize does not re-enter the developer/QA loop for pre-existing unrelated failures.

title: Finalize only reruns validation on target drift
rationale: QA already validated the task; finalize should only rerun npm test when the target branch revision changed after QA. Persisting QA target/head refs in run progress lets finalize distinguish no-drift pushes from true drift verification.

title: Finalize integration uses intent-based command naming
rationale: The finalize step is meant to bring target-branch drift onto the task branch for validation, not to prescribe rebase as the architectural policy. Renaming FinalizeCommands.rebaseCommand to integrateTargetCommand and the prompt variable to vcsIntegrateTargetCommand keeps backend behavior flexible while matching finalize's real purpose.

title: Finalize skip-vs-rerun is runtime-enforced
rationale: Pipeline-executor now records the current target ref before finalize verdict handling and validates FINALIZE_VALIDATION.md against the drift expectation. If target refs match, finalize must mark Test Validation as SKIPPED; if target drift exists, finalize may not skip validation. This prevents prompt drift or agent mistakes from bypassing the finalize drift contract.

title: JJ head resolution should ignore ephemeral scratch children
rationale: In colocated jj repos, bookmark moves and git-imports can leave the default workspace on an unbookmarked empty child commit while the real branch tip sits on @-. JujutsuBackend.getHeadId() now prefers the parent change when @ is unbookmarked but @- carries bookmarks, so finalize/refinery runtime checks reason about the effective branch tip instead of the scratch working-copy child.

description: A live bd-ca19 rerun showed '[foreman] Auto-labeled bd-ca19 with branch:HEAD' even after earlier branch-label sanitization work. Dispatcher was still detecting currentBranch through a raw GitBackend path before workspace creation, which returned detached HEAD in this colocated jj repo.
resolution: Use VcsBackendFactory.create({backend:"auto"}) for dispatch-time branch detection and reject invalid branch labels like HEAD before auto-labeling.

description: Finalize retry suppression missed artifacts that used '## Failure Scope Analysis' with '### Classification: UNRELATED_FILES'. That caused no-drift finalize contract failures with unrelated test failures to loop back to developer even though the failure was meant to be terminal/non-retryable.
resolution: Extend parseFinalizeFailureScope() to recognize analysis/classification forms and cover the case with a pipeline retry regression test.

description: Finalize can fail on unrelated rebase conflicts when a task commit contains transient artifacts like TEST_RESULTS.md.
resolution: If the task branch is unpushed, save the intended diff, reset the task branch to origin/main, reapply only the intended task files, recommit, then rebase/push to verify finalizeability.

description: Validate external CRD/API objects against the real API server before trusting mock-backed tests: a hand-written mock accepts shapes the server rejects. Four invalid shapes passed unit tests here — a kelos Task missing required 'credentials', volumes at spec.volumes instead of spec.worker.podOverrides.volumes, TaskBudget.spec.period as a string instead of an object, and workerPoolRef combined with mutually-exclusive fields. Each was caught only by 'kubectl apply --dry-run=server' against the installed CRD. Same class as stubbing a VCS: the stub accepted a bare branch name where real git needs origin/<branch>, and a conflictingFiles field that does not exist on MergeResult.
resolution: Dry-run every generated object against the live CRD (kubectl apply --dry-run=server) before relying on unit tests, and exercise VCS seams against real repositories in an integration test. Encode each discovered constraint so it cannot regress: make the field required in the options type rather than optional, and cite the dry-run in a comment on the assertion.

description: A crashing Elixir GenServer reports its failure as the ABSENCE of activity, not as an error. ForemanServer.Scheduler.age_seconds/2 clause-matched nil/DateTime/binary but not NaiveDateTime, which is what the Postgres read model returns for updated_at — so every 5s tick raised FunctionClauseError in active_runs/0 and terminated the process. Two tells both pointed away from the real cause: the /scheduler/tick endpoint returned 500 with an EMPTY BODY, and scheduler state reported last_tick: nil, which reads as 'never started' rather than 'dies on every tick'. coerce_datetime/1 in projection_store.ex already handled the naive case, so this was a missed clause on a known shape.
resolution: Add the %NaiveDateTime{} clause reading the value as Etc/UTC. When a scheduler or poller appears idle, read the server logs for a GenServer terminating before believing it never ran; and when one datetime helper handles a shape, grep sibling helpers for the same clause set.

description: A capacity/slot accounting bug can hide behind a health flag that is computed but never consumed. ForemanServer.Scheduler counted ALL active_runs toward max_concurrent while the 'stale' flag it already calculated went unused, and nothing sweeps stale runs (RecoveryEngine only reconciles an observation pushed to it, it never polls) — so an abandoned run's slot was never released and dispatch silently stopped. The subtlety that makes the naive fix wrong: WorkerHeartbeat does NOT bump run.updated_at (only phase transitions do), so a single long phase looks stale by timestamp while its worker is alive. On the live cluster a dead run read updated_at ~42m but heartbeat_age 12.4h.
resolution: Count capacity over live runs only, but judge staleness on heartbeat age with updated_at as fallback, and keep reporting every active run so stale ones stay visible. When a projection already computes a health/stale flag, grep for its consumers — a flag with no reader is a bug waiting to surface.

description: A failing step that does not BLOCK is the hardest kind to notice. Foreman's Node assumption had four sites; three were found one at a time by live runs. The fourth (npm ci + npx tsc --noEmit in the finalize builtin) survived all three rounds because it only wrote 'FAILED' into FINALIZE_REPORT.md without failing the pipeline — so every non-Node report carried two false failures indistinguishable from real ones. Related: npm ci REQUIRES a lockfile (fails on manifest-only Node projects), and npx tsc without a tsconfig.json tries to FETCH a package rather than typecheck.
resolution: Skip inapplicable steps and report SKIPPED, not SUCCESS, so 'nothing to do' stays distinguishable from 'passed'. Write the end-to-end test across ALL sites of a shared assumption at once, and pin the opposite direction too — a skip-everything implementation satisfies every negative assertion.

name: probe-projection-shape-for-event-sourced-fixtures
description: When writing a test fixture against an event-sourced projection, probe the resulting projection shape instead of trusting the event payload you wrote. Two Foreman examples that each silently produced a fixture testing nothing: RunFailed stamps run.failed_at from the EVENT's occurred_at and ignores a payload failed_at, so backdating via payload records every failure as 'now' (expiry untestable); and a run's task_id is populated only by RunStarted, so a run recorded via RunFailed alone is not attributable to its task, making a 4-failure fixture count as 1 and computing the wrong backoff window. Fix: write a throwaway test dumping Map.keys/values of the projection entry, build the fixture from what is actually stored, and emit the same event sequence a real run does (RunStarted before RunFailed) rather than only the terminal event.

When a layered prompt injects guidance that contradicts the shared prompt it wraps, the later and more specific instruction wins - and a stronger model can mask the conflict entirely by resolving it correctly. A kelos documentation phase went STUCK on a missing DOCUMENTATION_REPORT.md because the report-shim guidance ('Foreman's reports directory is not writable, upload instead') was placed BEFORE the phase prompt, which then said: Create the directory first with mkdir -p "{{reportDir}}". MiniMax obeyed the mkdir, hit 'mkdir: cannot create directory /home/foreman: Permission denied', announced it would look for the shim, and never issued the call - reporting the phase blocked. claude-haiku had resolved the identical conflict correctly (it called the shim 3x), so the failure read as MiniMax flakiness. It was not: the run that passed was a different workflow (nodeless pins documentation to Haiku; smoke and default both pin it to MiniMax). Model-correlated intermittency in prompt-driven behavior is a conflict signal, not flakiness - diff the workflow's model pins before blaming the model.
resolution: Append injected guidance AFTER the wrapped prompt so it is the last word, and have it NAME and overrule the specific conflicting instruction ('ignore any instruction above telling you to mkdir -p that directory') rather than hinting indirectly that the directory is unwritable. Also state that the expected error is not a blocker, or the agent reports the phase blocked on seeing it. Fix in the INJECTING seam, not the shared prompt, when the shared text is correct for its other consumers: reportDir is real and writable on the local path (pi-sdk-tools ensureReportDir mkdirs it) and prompt-loader REQUIRED_PROMPT_MARKERS pins {{reportDir}}/DOCUMENTATION_REPORT.md, so deleting the line would break local runs to fix pod runs. Verify by asserting RELATIVE ORDERING in the assembled Task.spec.prompt, and teeth-check the ordering assertion and the wording assertion INDEPENDENTLY - reverting one must fail only its own test, or one assertion silently covers the other's seam.

content: When a workflow/config is safe because of what it LACKS rather than what it declares, add a test asserting the absence — otherwise nothing protects it. The explore workflow cannot push only because finalize/create-pr/pr-wait/merge/merge-resolver are absent; a prompt will not stop a push, and the tool policy cannot either since the pod-side hook fails open by design. Every existing bundled-workflow gate asserted PRESENCE, so the safety property was invisible to the suite and one appended phase away from silently disappearing. Two corroborating details: the file's own header advertised a '-> Finalize' pipeline it deliberately omitted (a stale copy-paste actively contradicting the safety property), and the presence-oriented gate had to be RELAXED to admit the file at all — which is precisely the moment to add the absence test, since relaxing a gate is what creates the hole.

description: The workflow YAML's tools.allowed is NOT the tool-policy authority -- foreman_server's overwatch.ex is, and it carries phase-specific rules the YAML does not express. overwatch.ex:320 denies the explorer bash/find/ls ('explorer must use Grep/Glob/Read discovery'); probing the live endpoint returns Bash=DENY for explorer but ALLOW for reviewer, documentation and qa, even though reviewer's YAML ALSO omits Bash. This produced two consecutive wrong diagnoses of the missing EXPLORER_REPORT.md in run f36967cb: first 'explorer lacks Bash in the tool policy' (right conclusion, wrong mechanism), then 'the hook fails open so the failure is behavioral -- the agent chose Write over the shim' (wrong: the deny is real and enforced). Both came from comparing YAML declarations against each other instead of asking the server. The consequence that mattered: the report shim's only invocation form is a shell pipeline, so a Bash-denied phase cannot upload a report at ANY prompt strength -- the a470dfb2 prompt-ordering fix repaired documentation and could never reach explorer.
resolution: Probe POST /worker/v1/tool-policy per phase x tool before reasoning about what a pod phase can do -- a phase's real capability is a server decision, not a config file. Corollary: any pod-side capability invoked as a shell command is unavailable to a Bash-denied phase regardless of prompt wording, so route it through a PreToolUse hook (which runs as a subprocess, not the Bash tool) instead.

description: execFileSync blocks the Node event loop, so an HTTP server created in the SAME process can never answer the subprocess's request -- every call times out. A hook test suite that ran the real shell hook against an in-process report server took 65s and failed with 'expected [] to have length 1', which reads as 'the hook never uploaded' when the hook was correct and only the harness was broken. Misleading detail: Node's own fetch() succeeds against the same server (it yields to the event loop), so the failure looks curl-specific and sends you chasing proxy env vars, ~/.curlrc, and ephemeral port ranges. Reproduced outside vitest to confirm it was not a test-runner quirk.
resolution: Drive subprocesses with async execFile (feed the payload via child.stdin.end(...) and resolve on 'close') whenever the same test also serves HTTP in-process; keep execFileSync only for paths that never touch the network. Diagnostic tell: a suite whose duration is a multiple of the subprocess's own timeout (3 x 20s here) -- that is a deadlock, not slow code.

name: Give a pod capability a non-shell route when policy can deny Bash
description: Any pod-side capability whose only invocation is a shell command is unreachable by a phase the tool policy denies Bash to, and no prompt wording can fix that. The report shim (cat <<EOF | sh report-shim.sh) was unreachable to the explorer for exactly this reason. The working shape is a PreToolUse hook that performs the side effect itself -- a hook runs as a subprocess of the agent runtime, NOT as the Bash TOOL, so the policy gate does not apply to it -- and then returns permissionDecision 'deny' with a permissionDecisionReason that tells the agent the work is already done. Verified live: the agent received 'Foreman uploaded EXPLORER_REPORT.md for you ... do not retry', reasoned 'the hook worked ... this is NOT a failure', and moved on. Deny is the honest verdict when the write genuinely cannot land; an 'allow' would leave the agent believing a local file exists. Match on the target LOCATION rather than a file-name pattern so every declared artifact is covered, and stay silent (exit 0, no JSON = 'no decision', which is NOT an allow) on everything else so the real policy gate still rules.

overwatch.ex's read gate called File.exists?/File.dir? in the SERVER process to judge paths belonging to an AGENT POD -- answering a question about the wrong machine. Live probe of the deployed server: /workspace/repo/InPulse.Api/Program.cs -> DENY 'read target does not exist', while /app/package.json -> ALLOW, because the latter happens to exist on the server. THAT ASYMMETRY IS THE DIAGNOSTIC SIGNATURE: if a gate allows server-local paths and denies target-local ones, it is testing the wrong filesystem. It denied Read for EVERY phase on the kelos backend, not just the explorer, and it presented as an agent behaving badly rather than a policy bug.

The compounding failure was a policy written against a tool vocabulary the runtime does not have: overwatch named Grep/Glob in four separate deny messages and blocked Bash to force their use, but Grep/Glob are not in the agent CLI's default tool set (verified from the session init event's tools array -- 25 tools, neither present) and the runtime's own error tells the agent to use grep/find via Bash instead. Requiring absent tools while forbidding present ones is unsatisfiable by construction. The result was a real run with ZERO code exploration, which the agent itself correctly described as a catch-22.
resolution: Branch the gate on caller ORIGIN, which was already on the wire (kelos-pretooluse:* for pod workers vs node-pipeline-policy:* for the in-process pipeline that shares this disk): skip filesystem checks for remote callers, keep them where the worker shares the filesystem. Before writing a policy that NAMES a tool, verify that tool exists in the target runtime by reading the session init event's tools array. Enforce read-only by rejecting state-changing FORMS -- write redirects first, since 'grep x y > out' defeats any binary allowlist -- rather than by allowlisting binaries.

name: Reach an unconfigurable vendor binary through the PATH via a pre-start hook
description:
When a vendor CLI's behavior is only settable by a command-line flag, and the harness invoking it forwards no flags, check whether the directory that RESOLVES the binary is writable and precedes the real one. In the kelos agent image the pod resolves 'claude' through /home/claude/.local/bin before /usr/bin, and that directory ships EMPTY and WRITABLE -- so a Task.spec.preCommands entry (a channel foreman already used for three shims) installs a wrapper there that re-execs the real binary with the flag added. Verified live in the pool pod: 27 tools with Grep and Glob present, and Write/Edit/Bash all still there.

Three details that fail SILENTLY and so are worth pinning in tests:
1. Re-exec by ABSOLUTE path (/usr/bin/claude). A bare 'claude' resolves back to the wrapper and recurses.
2. Prefer the ADDITIVE flag. --allowed-tools ADDS to the default tool set; --tools REPLACES it, so --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob" yields exactly those four and strips Write, Edit and Task.
3. Write the wrapper UNCONDITIONALLY every Task. A pooled worker's filesystem persists across every Task it serves (per the preCommands CRD docs), so a conditional install lets an earlier Task's wrapper keep supplying different flags.

kelos-client.test.ts read preCommands[0] as its definition of 'a baseline was captured'. Appending any new preCommand broke it -- but the deeper problem is that [0] encoded the WRONG invariant. The baseline capture must be LAST, not first: it records the worktree state the returned patch is diffed against, so every install that could touch the worktree has to run BEFORE it. So the old assertion would have passed happily while the real ordering requirement was violated (a baseline captured first, with worktree-touching installs after it, silently excludes their changes from the patch). The test looked like it guarded ordering and guarded nothing.
resolution: Locate the entry by CONTENT (findIndex on a distinguishing substring), then assert the ordering property explicitly -- here expect(idx).toBe(length - 1). Teeth-check by moving the entry off the end. Heuristic: a test that breaks merely because you APPENDED to a list is telling you it pinned a position instead of a meaning; the fix is to name the invariant, not to renumber the index.

description:
A wiring test asserted the source matched /cancellationReason\(/ to prove the phase loop consulted a new cancellation check. It proved nothing: the helper's own 'export function cancellationReason(' satisfies that pattern, so DELETING the entire loop consultation left the test GREEN. The test claimed to prove wiring and only proved the function existed.

This is the third instance of the same shape in one day: (1) here, definition-satisfies-use-assertion; (2) a test indexing preCommands[0] as its definition of 'a baseline was captured', which broke on any append AND encoded the wrong invariant (baseline must be LAST); (3) mulch mx-8134d3, where a PreToolUse hook was verified as WRITTEN to a path nothing read, so every unit test passed while the gate never fired. Grep-based structural tests are especially prone to this because a definition and its call site nearly always share a substring.
resolution: Assert on a token that appears ONLY at the call site -- here ctx.checkCancelled( , since the declaration is 'checkCancelled?:' and cannot match it. Then assert the RELATIONSHIP rather than presence: index arithmetic requiring the consult point to fall after 'while (i < phases.length) {' and before 'const agentName = ...', so the check must be inside the loop AND before dispatch. Always teeth-check by deleting the wiring and confirming the test fails with the expected message. GENERAL RULE: when a test asserts that A uses B, make sure the assertion cannot be satisfied by B alone.

name: ACP protocol constraints for the phase backend
description: ACP's permission gate only sees mutations, and it carries no model parameter. Verified live against claude-agent-acp 0.64.2: session/request_permission fires for writes (a denied Write never reached disk) but NOT for reads or read-only terminal commands, in any of its five permission modes (default/acceptEdits/plan/dontAsk/bypassPermissions). So AcpClient.enforcesToolPolicy means 'mutations are gated', not 'every tool call is gated' — a phase needing read-gating cannot get it from this backend. Separately, ACP has no in-protocol model selection: NewSessionRequest is only cwd/additionalDirectories/mcpServers/_meta, PromptRequest has no override, session modes are permissions not models, and the session/select_model proposal (PR #182) was closed unmerged. Per-phase model routing therefore rides the spawn env (ANTHROPIC_MODEL), which the adapter honours over settings — portable by convention at the process boundary, not by spec.

An out-of-process agent runtime's own accounting fields cannot be taken at face value — unit tests pass while the numbers are wrong by orders of magnitude. Three defects survived 33 green tests and only surfaced on the first live run: (1) counting ACP agent_message_chunk notifications as turns reported 28 turns for a 2-turn phase, because ACP emits one chunk per text delta — turns must be counted on message BOUNDARIES; this feeds the maxTurns gate and budget. (2) Reading PromptResponse.usage.inputTokens alone reported 23 tokens for a phase billing 195k: inputTokens counts only the UNCACHED prompt, so cachedReadTokens (39k) and cachedWriteTokens (91k) must be summed in, and since cache-write is ~12.5x cache-read this is the dominant cost driver. Note usage is marked UNSTABLE in the v1 schema, UsageUpdate's used/size are CONTEXT-window tokens rather than per-turn in/out, and its cost.amount is CUMULATIVE (take the latest, never sum). (3) SIGTERMing the adapter tore the pipe down under an in-flight write and it died on unhandled EPIPE. Lesson: for any new runtime backend, do one live run and reconcile turns/tokens/cost against the provider before trusting the adapter.
resolution: Turn counting moved into the accumulator keyed on message boundaries (a tool_call closes the message); acpTokenAccounting() sums inputTokens + cachedReadTokens + cachedWriteTokens; teardown destroys stdout and ends stdin so the adapter observes EOF, with the SIGTERM kept as an unref'd 250ms backstop. All three now covered by tests and re-verified on a live Bedrock run (turns 28 to 2, tokensIn 23 to 195342, no EPIPE).

title: ACP gate cost scales with writes, so the MCP tool port is unblocked
rationale: Measured rather than assumed: per-call gate latency was the one risk that could have made an out-of-process policy gate untenable and wasted the whole MCP port. A live run showed the gate fires per WRITE, not per tool call, so the cost is bounded by mutations.

description: A test suite can merge RED and stay red for days, and the surfaced error names the wrong culprit at every layer. Five failures on this branch had three unrelated causes, each masking the next. (1) 'as never' on a partial mock literal is the enabling defect: { name, rebase } as never compiled fine while the executor also called getFinalizeCommands, so the pipeline threw 'is not a function' before reaching the code under test. Never cast a partial mock of a wide interface — build it from a shared factory so one interface addition fixes every consumer. (2) With the TypeError cleared, rebase fired 3x not 1x — NOT a rebase bug but qaReportHasTestEvidence, a gate added AFTER the tests, rejecting a bare '## Verdict: PASS' so retryOnFail looped the phase twice more. A count assertion that is off by exactly the retry limit should point at a verdict gate, not at the thing being counted. (3) toHaveBeenCalledWith matches only the FIRST call: with expect.anything() as arg 1 and a null mail client on the earlier phase-started call, it failed before the kind was compared, hiding that production was correct all along. Filter mock.calls for the call you mean. Diagnosis method that paid off: run the test at the commit that introduced it (git worktree add --detach <sha>) to prove pre-existing rather than assuming, and print the real intermediate state (phase order, sendMail kinds, validator error) instead of reasoning from the assertion message.
resolution: MergeValidator scopes --typeRoots to the temp dir when the checker is tsc, with a companion test asserting invalid TypeScript is STILL rejected so the fix cannot degrade into no checking. The VcsBackend mock factory was promoted from conflict-resolver-vcs.test.ts to a shared __tests__/vcs-backend-mock.ts covering the full interface (it cannot live in src/test-support/, which ships in the build and so cannot import vitest). QA stub reports now use the gate's sanctioned 'Test suite: SKIPPED'.

description: Three separate red tests on this branch shared one root cause: production code and tests reading state OUTSIDE the repository, so results varied per machine and the red was never trusted. (a) MergeValidator ran 'tsc --noEmit' on a file in os.tmpdir(); tsc resolves ambient @types by walking UP, so a broken @types/glob+minimatch in /home/<user>/node_modules failed validation for valid TypeScript — the home directory decided whether a merge-conflict resolution was accepted. (b) resolveWorkflowName consults ~/.foreman/workflows/, so tests asserting 'removed task types fall back to default' failed on any machine whose foreman init predated the removal of chore/docs/question. FOREMAN_HOME already existed as the override hook, unused. (c) 'git config get <key>' is a git>=2.46 subcommand; on git 2.43 it errors 'key does not contain a section: get' and the surrounding try/catch treated that as 'not configured', silently demoting a git-town user's trunk so Foreman rebased onto the wrong branch. Two lessons: when a bug is version- or environment-conditional, a behavioural test cannot catch it on machines where the condition is absent — assert on the SOURCE instead (this shipped in two backends at once because the jujutsu suite skipIfs away entirely without jj installed, hiding 55 tests). And always grep for the same call shape elsewhere after fixing one instance; the sibling had it verbatim.
resolution: GitBackend and JujutsuBackend use 'git config --get'; a source-level assertion in no-direct-git.test.ts now forbids the space form in both, verified by reintroducing it and confirming red. resolve-workflow-name.test.ts points FOREMAN_HOME at an empty temp dir for the suite. MergeValidator scopes --typeRoots to its temp dir.

description: A skipIf'd or bare-skipped test is invisible debt that hides real bugs — and most skips are stale, not obsolete. 68 of 90 skips in this repo gated on the  binary being absent, which is exactly how a git-town config bug shipped in jujutsu-backend.ts unnoticed (its sibling in git-backend.ts was caught only because that suite runs). Installing jj immediately surfaced 3 genuine failures. Two reusable lessons. (1) jj keeps its OWN user identity and does not read git's user.name/user.email; a fixture that only sets git config produces authorless commits and  refuses them ('Won't push commit <id> since it has no author and/or committer set'). Set JJ_USER/JJ_EMAIL on the INIT call —  afterwards only affects later commits, since init itself creates the working-copy commit, and jj warns 'The author of the working copy will stay <>'. (2) A bare describe.skip with no reason is worse than a failing test: nobody can distinguish obsolete from stale. 15 of 21 skipped auto-merge tests passed the moment they were run. When re-skipping is genuinely right, state the blocker — here autoMerge builds ElixirMergeQueue for a REGISTERED project, so the local-queue dequeue mock the tests configure is never consulted. Also recurring: a mock method added to a hoisted constructor is silently dropped if resetMocks calls mockImplementation, which REPLACES it — add to both.
resolution: jj repos get identity via JJ_USER/JJ_EMAIL on the init call (plus repo-local config for later backend-run operations); 15 auto-merge tests un-skipped after adding updateTaskStatus to BOTH MockForemanStore definitions and re-pointing assertions from enqueueSetTaskStatus to store.updateTaskStatus; the last 4 re-skipped WITH a stated reason (needs an ElixirMergeQueue stub). Suite went from 90 skipped to 7.

content: A skipIf gate on a missing binary is a PASS in CI. vitest exits 0 reporting '17 passed | 55 skipped' when jj is absent, so a green check certified 55 tests that never ran — and that is exactly how a git-town config bug shipped in jujutsu-backend.ts while the identical line in git-backend.ts was caught (only the git suite executed). Installing the binary in CI fixes today, but the failure mode is silence, so a dropped toolchain step or a broken download reverts it invisibly. The durable half is a test asserting the binary exists when process.env.CI is set: a no-op on a contributor's machine, a loud ENOENT in CI. Verify such a guard by removing the binary from PATH under CI=true and confirming it fails. Also check the vitest config include/exclude lists before assuming the binary is the only gap — src/lib/vcs/__tests__ is EXCLUDED from vitest.unit.config.ts and runs only under vitest.integration.config.ts, so a tool installed for the wrong job changes nothing.

name: Serve in-process tools to an out-of-process agent over HTTP MCP
description: Re-expose in-process Pi ToolDefinitions to an out-of-process agent by serving the SAME objects over in-process HTTP MCP, not by reimplementing them. Three facts make this thin: (1) ToolDefinition.parameters is TypeBox, which already IS JSON Schema, so it becomes the MCP inputSchema verbatim and cannot drift from the tool; (2) the Claude ACP adapter advertises mcpCapabilities {http, sse} and NOT stdio, so the server runs in the worker process with the tools closing over the phase context — no runId/taskId/reportDir plumbing through subprocess env at all; (3) execute's real signature is (toolCallId, params, signal?, onUpdate?, ctx), so thread the AbortSignal for cancellation. Bind the listener BEFORE spawning the agent (session/new needs the URL) on an OS-assigned port (parallel phases each need one), and close it in a finally on every exit path or a failed phase leaks a listener per phase. Two protocol judgments: report a throwing tool as isError on the RESULT, never a JSON-RPC error, because the latter reads as 'server broken' and can abort the session; and surface control-flow tools (abort_phase/needs_retry) OUT-OF-BAND via a controlOutcome() getter, because over MCP a tool's return value is only text to the agent and the phase would otherwise continue straight past an abort — first signal wins so a later call cannot downgrade it. Verified live: the agent called mcp__foreman__artifact_write and the file landed via Foreman's own ToolDefinition; abort_phase returned {type: ABORTED} to the runner.

Killing an agent that may be mid-git leaves the worktree PERMANENTLY wedged, and the retry hits the same wall. A stale .git/index.lock makes every subsequent git command in that repository fail with 'Another git process seems to be running' — so a phase interrupted during a checkpointPr commit/push does not just fail, it poisons the worktree for every later attempt. Neither git-backend.ts nor doctor.ts recovers a stale lock. Two things make the fix correct rather than merely effective. First, ORDERING is the safety property: locks may only be cleared after the child has provably exited, because clearing one while the process still lives could delete a LIVE lock and corrupt a commit in progress — so the test drives a real EOF-ignoring process (sleep) and asserts process.kill(pid,0) throws ESRCH at clear time, and removing the reap makes it red. Second, in a git WORKTREE — where every Foreman phase runs —  is a FILE containing 'gitdir: <path>', not a directory, so checking <worktree>/.git/index.lock misses every real case; resolve the pointer first. Generalizes to any harness that SIGTERMs a child which might hold a resource lock: wait for the exit, then clean, and test the ordering rather than just the cleanup.
resolution: Teardown awaits reapChild (EOF -> SIGTERM at 250ms -> SIGKILL at 2s, resolving either way so teardown cannot hang), THEN calls clearStaleGitLocks. Lock discovery resolves the gitdir pointer so it works in a worktree, checks index.lock/HEAD.lock/config.lock, and never throws since it runs in a finally. Verified on a genuinely wedged repo: git add failed, a phase cleared the lock, git add succeeded.

content: Foreman resolves workflow shorthands to Pi-style ids (anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5), which an out-of-process provider need not accept — Bedrock rejects that exact id with '400 The provided model identifier is invalid'. Any backend routing phases to a foreign provider therefore needs a map (FOREMAN_ACP_MODEL_MAP, mirroring kelos's KELOS_MODEL_MAP/gatewayModel). The load-bearing rule: once any mapping exists, an UNMAPPED id fails the phase instead of passing through. Substituting or passing through silently changes the cost and quality the workflow asked for, and a P0 phase configured for opus quietly served by haiku is worse than one that refuses to start — this is the same fail-closed principle as a safety gate. Three implementation details that matter: split each entry on the FIRST '=' only (Bedrock targets contain ':' and provider ids contain '/' and '.'); reject a half-written entry rather than ignoring it, since an entry that silently fails to apply resurfaces as a provider 400 mid-phase; and translate BEFORE spawning anything, so an unmapped model costs no API call. Report the failure as the pipeline's own error convention (agent-error) rather than throwing — an exception escaping a phase backend takes down the worker and loses the run's bookkeeping.

name: ACP backend full-chain verification result
description: The ACP backend runs a real explorer -> developer -> QA chain end to end against claude-agent-acp on Bedrock, verified 2026-08-04. Each phase succeeded with the workflow-native model id through FOREMAN_ACP_MODEL_MAP, wrote its gating artifact via mcp__foreman__artifact_write, and handed off to the next: explorer 4 turns/6 tools, developer 4/4 (filesChanged correctly reported ['src/math.js'] and  really landed in the file), qa 4/4 calling mcp__foreman__safe_command_run then validation_result then artifact_write. Total ~/bin/bash.47 at haiku. What the chain surfaced that unit tests could not: a QA report can satisfy parseVerdict (pass) while FAILING qaReportHasTestEvidence, because that gate requires a runner command AND numeric pass/fail counts — 'npm test' plus 'All tests passed successfully' is rejected. The pipeline then overrides the verdict to fail and burns the developer retries. This was a HARNESS defect, not a backend or foreman one: the real bundled prompt (src/defaults/prompts/default/qa.md:54) does specify the required shape, '- Test suite: X passed, Y failed | SKIPPED', and re-running with that instruction produced '- Test suite: 1 passed, 0 failed' and hasTestEvidence=true. Lesson for any future phase-runner backend: verify artifacts against the REAL gate functions (parseVerdict AND qaReportHasTestEvidence from roles.js), not just artifact existence, and drive phases with the bundled prompts rather than ad-hoc ones — an ad-hoc prompt that omits a format requirement produces a plausible artifact the pipeline rejects.

A feature can be fully built and terminate one step short of working, and the missing step is invisible because every piece it needs already exists. Foreman's ask_operator parked a run at waiting_for_operator, and nothing ever resumed it: the worker set only the RUN status while the scheduler dispatches on TASK status (only ready/approved are dispatchable, and nativeTaskStatusForPhase leaves every task at in-progress). Separately, an operator.resume COMMAND, an operator_intervention aggregate with a state machine, HumanInterruptionRecorded/InteractiveRecoveryResumed events, and projection handling for them ALL existed — but the projection wrote only interactive_recovery, phase_status and recovery_next_action, and grepping showed recovery_next_action is read by nobody. So the run status stayed parked and the design dead-ended in the projection. Diagnostic method that found it: trace the full causal chain from the parked state to the thing that would un-park it, and grep each intermediate field for a CONSUMER — a field that is written and never read is the signature of a chain that terminates early. Also: when writing tests against an event-sourced projection, verify the event type names against the source (grep for the quoted strings) before seeding; I invented RunStatusChanged/TaskStatusChanged, which do not exist — the real ones are RunUpdated/TaskUpdated — and a seed built on nonexistent events would have made the test vacuous.
resolution: Worker parks the TASK at 'blocked' (not just the run) when waiting; the projection lifts run waiting_for_operator -> pending and task blocked -> ready on InteractiveRecoveryResumed, keyed through the run's task_id since the event carries only run_id. Interruptions deliberately stay parked. Verified by injecting removal of both calls and watching the same 2 tests go red.
